items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been located. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

items.exhaustive_search_summary: Searched all four federal censuses in which Elizabeth appears (1850 Jasper Co., with the original image examined; 1860 and 1870 Smith Co.; 1880 Raleigh, Smith Co.). Also searched her daughters' censuses that report a mother's birthplace (Sarah Martha Lovett 1880; Amanda Ainsworth 1880 [original line checked], 1900, 1910), the 1850 Turnbow households in Mississippi (FAN), the Mississippi Death Certificate Index 1912-1943 (daughters not found), the Find a Grave index (no memorial found), and the LDS Mississippi District minutes attached in the tree (no mention). Not searched: original images of the 1860/1870/1880 Barker entries, a true LDS record-of-members register, newspapers, Confederate pension files, and any Alabama county source naming a birth county. Alabama did not require birth registration until 1908.
items.narrative_markdown:
# Birthplace of Elizabeth Mariah (Turnbow) Barker (c. 1823)

**Conclusion (Probable):** Elizabeth, wife of the English-born blacksmith and farmer Jonathan Barker of Jasper and Smith counties, Mississippi, was born about 1823 in **Alabama**, not England. The FamilySearch tree records her as Elizabeth Mariah Turnbow (KWJ6-RPH). The "England" birthplace attached to her comes from an indexing error.

**Project recap — Patrick Flynn, b. ca. 1845 Ireland, d. 1908 Schuylkill County, PA**

The existing project had already established, at a **probable** level, that Patrick is the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, based on the 1850 and 1860 US censuses (Patrick in Thomas's household) and the 1908 death certificate (naming Thomas Flynn as father). Both the 1850 and 1860 censuses record Patrick's birthplace as **Ireland** — the death certificate's conflicting Pennsylvania entry was attributed to secondary-informant error by the son-in-law informant.

---

**What the Irish-origins research will pursue**

Because Patrick was only about five years old in the 1850 census, his arrival almost certainly occurred between 1845 and 1850 — the heart of the Famine emigration wave. The most productive record sets to search are:

1. **US passenger arrival records (1845–1850)** — Philadelphia, New York, Baltimore, and Boston ports. Thomas Flynn would be the head of household to search; Patrick would appear as a child. Castle Garden did not open until 1855, so the relevant records are pre-immigration-station manifests.
2. **Naturalization records** — Thomas Flynn's declaration of intent and/or petition for naturalization would name his county or townland of birth in Ireland. Schuylkill County Court of Common Pleas naturalization records and NARA's Eastern District of Pennsylvania records are the primary targets.
3. **Later US census entries** — The 1880 census asked for parents' birthplaces (state or country), and the 1900 census asked for year of immigration and years in the US. Any of those for Patrick, Thomas, or siblings Mary and James Flynn may narrow the Irish county.
4. **Irish records** — Griffith's Valuation (surveyed county by county, 1847–1864) and the Tithe Applotment Books (1823–1837) are the main surviving pre-Famine name indexes. Civil registration began in Ireland in 1864, too late for Patrick's birth, but Catholic parish registers (many digitized on IrishGenealogy.ie and Registers of Ireland) predate that.
5. **Schuylkill County neighbors** — Chain migration was common; Schuylkill County's anthracite mining communities drew heavily from specific Irish counties (Clare, Galway, Mayo, Roscommon, Tipperary). The surnames and birthplaces of Thomas Flynn's neighbors in 1850 and 1860 may point to the home county.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been located. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been located. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

Tree subject: I1 = William Jacob Honeyman (Male, d. 1783 Hutton Rudby), parents I2 (William Honniman) and I3 (Phillis Mackannel), wife I4 (Catherine Billingham Codling).

Key assertions:
- a_001: baptism 5 Apr 1719, Hutton Rudby — "William Hunnyman baptised" — child of William (src_001)

- a_005: christening 2 Dec 1716, Edinburgh — "William Honniman christened" — son of William Honniman and Elizabeth Duncan (src_004)
- a_006: relationship — "Child of William Honniman and Elizabeth Duncan" (from 1716 Edinburgh record, src_004) — shared with q_002
- a_007: burial 27 Mar 1783, Rudby — "Willm Honeyman buried" (src_005) — clearly I1
- a_008: birth c. Mar 1716-Mar 1717 (calculated from burial age 66, src_005) — clearly I1
- a_009: marriage 19 Jul 1738, Hutton Rudby — "William Huneman married Catherine Codling" (src_006) — clearly I1
- a_012: burial 22 Aug 1737, Hutton Rudby — "William Hunneman buried" (src_009) — this is the father I2
- a_013: burial 5 Apr 1783, Rudby — "Catherine, wife of Wm Honeyman, buried" (src_010) — this is wife I4

- a_015: marriage 20 Aug 1738, Rudby — bishop's transcript of the same marriage, William Hunneman to Catharine Codling (src_006) — clearly I1

**q_002 — Where did father William Hunniman originate? Is the Scoonie, Fife tree record his?**
- a_002: same as above — child of William (father role)
- a_006: same as above — child of William Honniman and Elizabeth Duncan
- a_010: burial 9 May 1738, Rudby — "Phyllis Hunneman buried" (src_007) — this is I3 (Phillis Mackannel/Hunneman)

The 1716 Edinburgh christening (a_005, a_006) gives William's mother as Elizabeth Duncan. The tree's father I2 (William Honniman) married Phillis Mackannel (I3). These are DIFFERENT women. Either:
(a) The Edinburgh William is a completely different person (different family, different mother), not the same as the Hutton Rudby William — in which case a_005 and a_006 should be linked to a NEW stub person, not I1; OR
(b) There is some complexity (perhaps the Edinburgh William is a half-sibling, or a different William Honeyman entirely in Edinburgh whose record was misidentified).

items.question: Do independent records confirm or refute that the woman recorded as Mary A./Polly Burton in the 1850–1880 census records as Jahue B. Burton's wife in Pulaski County, Kentucky, is the same individual as Mary Ann Eastham, shown on the FamilySearch profile as Jahue B. Burton's wife?
items.rationale: Every fact about I2 (Mary Ann Eastham) derives solely from the FamilySearch collaborative tree (S1, quality 1 — compiled, unsourced). The census records already attached to Jahue B. Burton (1850, 1860, 1870, 1880) show his wife variously as 'Mary A Burton' and 'Polly Ann Burton' in Pulaski County; the FamilySearch profile assigns her birth surname 'Eastham' and a Greenup County, KY birth origin. After Jahue's 1898 death in Pulaski County, the profile places his wife in Boyd County (1900 residence, 1904 death, Fields Cemetery burial) — a geographically separate trajectory that raises a real possibility the FamilySearch profile merged two distinct women into one entry. Kentucky marriage records, Pulaski and Boyd county vital and probate records, and death/obituary sources can test whether a single woman's life history runs through both name forms and both counties, or whether the evidence supports two separate identities.

items.question: Do independent records confirm or refute that the woman recorded as Jahue B Burton's wife in Pulaski County, Kentucky census records from 1850 through 1880 — variously listed as 'Mary A Burton' and 'Polly Burton' — is the same individual as Mary Ann Eastham, born circa 1823 in Greenup County, Kentucky?
items.rationale: The FamilySearch Couple link between Jahue B Burton and Mary Ann Eastham rests entirely on the compiled FamilySearch Family Tree (quality 1), which has no independent source records attached to the Mary Ann Eastham persona. Census records 1850–1880 name Jahue's wife in Pulaski County as 'Mary A Burton' (1850, 1860) and 'Polly Ann / Polley A. P. Burton' (1870, 1880) — 'Polly' being a common diminutive of Mary. However, the birthplace data attached to I2 (Greenup County, northeastern KY) sits far from Pulaski County (south-central KY), and I2's death and burial are in Boyd County (also northeastern KY), raising the possibility that two women were incorrectly merged. Kentucky marriage records, early Greenup and Boyd County records, and Eastham family documentation are the primary avenues to confirm or refute the identity claim independently of the FamilySearch merge.

Burton's wife), both being children of a Virginia-born Eastham father and a Kentucky-born mother. The real conflict is between Robert's own 1880 census (a_144, Virginia) and Robert's own 1870 bond (a_159, Kentucky).
